# Whatever Comes to Me

The morning arrived like it always does—not with fanfare but with a quiet persistence, light creeping under the curtains whether I was ready for it or not. I've been thinking lately about how we don't get to negotiate with time. It just comes, and we either rise to meet it or we pull the covers over our heads.

I chose the covers this morning.

But here's what happens when you lie in bed with your thoughts: they multiply like rabbits in spring. Suddenly I'm thinking about my friend Marcus who hasn't called in three months, and whether that means something or nothing. I'm thinking about the email I need to send but keep rewording in my head, never satisfied with the tone. I'm thinking about my mother's voice on the phone yesterday, how she said everything was fine but it didn't sound fine. The way people do that—they lie with the truth.

There's a coffee shop I pass sometimes where they have this particular barista who always remembers orders. Not in a creepy way, but in that genuinely kind way that makes you feel seen. I wonder if that's what people are really starving for these days—not coffee or recognition, but just to be remembered. To matter enough that someone holds a detail about you in their mind.

I read somewhere that we're living through the age of unprecedented loneliness, even as we're more connected than ever. Someone had to coin a phrase for that, which means somewhere, someone felt it too, deeply enough to make it a thing. To name it. Sometimes naming something makes it hurt less, or maybe it just hurts differently.

My neighbor has a dog that barks at nothing. Or at everything. I suspect it's probably something—just something invisible to me. Some frequency only dogs can hear, some presence or memory or fear. I've started to wonder if we're all like that. Barking at things other people can't perceive, responding to invisible forces, our behavior seeming irrational to everyone but us.

I thought about starting a journal where I only wrote things I actually meant, not things I thought I was supposed to mean. But then I realized I'm not always sure which is which. We internalize expectations so thoroughly that sometimes our genuine desires become indistinguishable from our programming. It's like asking someone to point out which drops of water in the ocean are the ones they personally poured in.

There's this thing that happens on certain afternoons when the light hits just right, and the whole world looks like a photograph from another era. Like we're all actors in a movie someone's already watched and will watch again. Those moments make me feel both insignificant and absolutely essential, as if the fact that I witnessed that particular arrangement of light and shadow matters infinitely and not at all.

I've been trying to be kinder, which sounds simple but is surprisingly difficult. It's not the grand gestures—I think most of us are reasonably good at those. It's the moment-to-moment stuff. The way you respond to someone's joke that wasn't funny. Whether you actually listen or just wait for your turn to speak. Whether you remember that someone mentioned their anxiety about something and follow up about it days later.

Kindness requires this persistent, boring attentiveness that our culture doesn't really value. We valorize grand romantic gestures and bold career moves, but the quiet work of consistently showing up for people, really hearing them, letting them be complicated—that's not the stuff of stories. And yet it's the stuff of actual life.

I wonder what future historians will say about us. Will they understand why we were so angry all the time? Will they get that we were scared? That we were living in the gap between the world we wanted and the world we had, and that gap was suffocating? Or will they think we were just ungrateful and neurotic?

Maybe both can be true.

I've noticed that I repeat myself sometimes—the same worries, the same small triumphs, the same failures. I used to think that meant I wasn't growing, but I'm starting to suspect it just means I'm human. We're all moving in spirals, not straight lines. We return to the same places but at different altitudes, with slightly better equipment, marginally more wisdom.

There's something about writing—about this particular act of arranging words in a sequence and hoping they mean something—that feels like the closest I get to honesty. Maybe because the page doesn't interrupt. It doesn't offer platitudes or advice. It just waits.

I'm tired, if I'm being honest. Not just tired of things—tired of the effort of existing in a world that rewards hustle and produces anxiety. Tired of deciding what to wear and what to say and whether to respond to that message or let it sit a little longer. Tired of the weight of potential, of all the things I could be doing and therefore the guilt about what I'm actually doing.

But also, underneath the tired, there's this curious energy. This sense that despite everything, despite the chaos and uncertainty and the way nothing ever goes quite according to plan, life is still generating moments of beauty. Still producing kindness. Still making jokes that aren't funny but matter because someone shared them with me.

And maybe that's enough. Not sufficient, not complete, but enough to justify getting out of bed tomorrow, and the day after, and however many days I get.

The light is different now than when I started thinking all this. Time moves like that—invisible and relentless and absolute. We can't stop it or even really slow it down. We can only decide what to do while we're here, in the middle of it, making our small choices, remembering people's names, listening to dogs bark at invisible things, trying to be kind.

That's what comes to me, anyway, this morning and the next.
